To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The effects of sulfur dioxide on western larch growth in the vicinity of Trail, B.C. were detected in tree-ring chronologies, and that the effects were most pronounced during the 1960s.
1. The effects of sulfur dioxide pollution on western larch ( Larix occidentalis Nutt.) are evident in the tree-ring records of five stands located near the lead–zine smelter at Trail.

(1) tree-ring width chronologies from polluted stands were significantly correlated with sulfur emissions from the smelter; (2) the relationship between tree-ring width variation and sulfur emissions was stronger for the years prior to installation of two tall emission stacks in 1958 than for the years following installation; and (3) tree-ring variation in polluted stands was significantly correlated with sulfur dioxide concentrations measured at a nearby site.

the relationship between the growth of trees and sulfur dioxide pollution.
the effect of sulfur dioxide emissions on tree-ring growth.
the effects of atmospheric pollution on forest ecosystems in the southern interior of British Columbia.

the effects of the Trail smelter on the growth of western larch are complex and difficult to interpret.

tree-ring chronologies can be used to detect and quantify the effects of sulfur pollution on tree growth.
the tree-ring record of sulfur deposition can be used to reconstruct past atmospheric sulfur emissions.
tree rings can be a useful tool for assessing the impacts of air pollution.
